items.recommendation: Set the deep-tier floor at 4 tok/s decode, measured at an 8k-token context (Phase 3's 8k point, at least 128 generated tokens). It applies to whichever engine holds the Apex synthesis role: 0731 now, V4.1 in the T-30 trial. With DSpark, measure greedy for comparison with the published figures, then the node's own settings: 0.15 (Arthur, adversary scoring; also covers the 0.2 cross-checks), 0.6 (synthesis) and 1.0 (server default). The floor is judged on the slowest of them. 0731 at UD-Q8_K_XL is judged with DSpark off, as D-61 approved. At its measured 14-16 tok/s, V4.1 clears the floor 3.5-4 times over, so speed decides nothing in the trial and T-30's blind scores decide it.
reasons: Under a quality-first directive, a floor should mark where the Apex stops working for its job, and never rank models. The node itself sets that point: the 3,072-token deep synthesis (deep_think.py:406) against the 900 s that tasks/__init__.py:187 allows for 'one generation'. The engine swap happens inside the generation slot (api.py:1403-1404, :1608-1609), so the 900 s covers the swap, the prefill and the decode. A 50-85 s swap plus a healthy 40-55 s prefill of a 6-8k prompt leaves room for 3,072 tokens at 3.8-4.0 tok/s, hence 4 (INFERRED). The 900 s is a design figure, not a hard stop. The Celery client's read timeout is 2,700 s in all (1,800 s wait + 900 s), and the chat streamer allows 3,600 s per read. A floor-speed synthesis is therefore slow, but it does not fail.

In human time, 4 tok/s gives a 500-token reply in 2:05, a 1,500-2,500-token Deep Think answer in 6:15-10:25 and a full 3,072-token synthesis in 12:48 of decode. At the 7 tok/s projection the same figures are 1:11, 3:34-5:57 and 7:19; at V4.1's 14 tok/s they are 0:36, 1:47-2:59 and 3:39. max_tokens counts reasoning tokens, so at high effort a visible 500-token answer needs 500 tokens plus the reasoning trace (INFERRED).

A whole deep run takes about 63 min at the projections (GLM 13, DeepSeek 7) if every call uses its token budget, and about 36 min at half. At the floors (GLM 6, DeepSeek 4) it takes about 116 / 63 min. Both the doc's 15-30 min (9.1 table, L655) and the message the Principal sees (api.py:1367: '15 to 30' deep, '5 to 8' standard) are optimistic even at the projections (INFERRED).

The register says the node samples DeepSeek at 1.0, but that is only the server default for a request that carries no temperature and no persona. Arthur's persona runs at 0.15 (api.py:1407-1411), the adversary scoring at 0.15 (deep_think.py:73), the deep synthesis at 0.6 (deep_think.py:466) and the strong cross-checks at 0.2 (approval.py:387). The trial must therefore measure those settings, not 1.0 alone.

Without a drafter, temperature should barely move decode speed: sampling costs about 1 ms against 60-70 ms per token. One run at 0.6 confirms this. Temperature matters through DSpark's draft acceptance, which falls as temperature rises. With DSpark, the slowest production setting is therefore the highest temperature in use, and the greedy-only Lucebox and Framework figures overstate what the node would see (INFERRED).

What the V4.1 result means: about 14.3-14.8 tok/s without DSpark and 16.3-18.4 with it, measured at temperature 0 on a PRO 495 ('gorgon-halo') with DwarfStar. It is UNVERIFIED on this node. That is 3.5-4 times the floor and twice 0731's projection. Neither engine is near the floor, so a V4.1 that scores lower cannot win on speed, and a V4.1 that scores higher wins on quality.

If 0731 at UD-Q8_K_XL measures below 4 tok/s on Day 1, first check placement (D-33). A healthy Q8 projects 6.8-7.2 tok/s, and BF16 mat-vec has a Vulkan path at the pin, so a result below 4 points to a fault more than to the file. If placement is clean, the remedy is UD-Q4_K_XL from the approved relief order (D-11 (b): about 11 tok/s projected, KLD 0.0102). V4.1 is not the remedy until it wins T-30.

Prefill should have a floor too: 40 tok/s at the 8k point for GLM and DeepSeek (set with D-33). At that rate GLM needs about 13 min to read a 24k-token document and about 21 min for 32k, against 3.6-5.4 min at a healthy 100-150 tok/s. On DeepSeek, 40 tok/s puts a 6k scoring prompt at 2:23 (INFERRED, depth-decay fit with D about 19k).

items.recommendation: Set the per-seat decode floors at gpt-oss-120b 25, GLM-5.3-Flash 6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 4 and the router 20 tok/s. Each is stated at 8k context and checked against the slower of the two Phase 3 timing points, and only this absolute floor fails V10. Add a review line at 70% of the projection that raises a to-do and never fails, plus prefill floors (gpt-oss 200, GLM 40, DeepSeek 40 tok/s at 8k). Make placement checks the real CPU-fallback detector, because on this unified-memory chip a CPU-resident model can decode nearly as fast as mainline Vulkan.
reasons: A floor's job is to catch a broken engine and a seat too slow for its job, never to pick a model. Each floor is roughly half of the pessimistic healthy figure at 8k, checked against the seat's job: gpt-oss is the fast utility and every seat's fallback, GLM carries about seven seats and the Deep Think generator, DeepSeek's synthesis must fit the 900 s design slack, and the router runs before every request (INFERRED).

Only the absolute floor fails the gate; the fraction of the projection raises a to-do. The projections are other machines' measurements scaled by arithmetic, and failing on a fraction would bring back the v0.3.5 band rule that D-33 (c) withdrew.

The stakes are uneven. A false floor fail on GLM or DeepSeek defers it through V22 and sends its seats to gpt-oss-120b, a quality loss, so their floors leave about 48% and 35-38% margin below the pessimistic healthy figures. Only gpt-oss's fail blocks the Phase 3 gate, and its margin of about 34% rests on it being the best-measured engine.

The gpt-oss-120b projection of 57-60 tok/s describes the wrong file: it was computed for the Q8_0-trunk file (3.594 GB/token). The Day 1 F16-trunk file reads about 4.97-4.99 GB/token: 1.904 GB of routed experts, 1.91 GB of 16-bit attention and 1.16 GB of 16-bit output head. That gives about 41-44 tok/s, and about 38-40 at 8k (INFERRED). Hence a floor of 25, not 30.

Human time at the floors: a 500-token reply takes 20 s on gpt-oss, 1:23 on GLM and 2:05 on DeepSeek; a 2,500-token answer takes 1:40, 6:57 and 10:25. The router at 20 tok/s returns an 80-token verdict in 4 s (10 s for the 200-token maximum) (INFERRED).

Speed floors cannot see whole-model CPU fallback here. CPU decode tops out at about 108 GB/s effective, which puts the CPU ceilings at gpt-oss about 21.7 tok/s, GLM 8.2, DeepSeek 6.3 and the router 24. Placement must be checked directly: all layers offloaded, a GTT delta of at least 0.85 x the weights, and the model buffer on Vulkan0 (INFERRED).

An op that falls to the CPU and copies weights runs about 40 times slower (Mistral-Small-4: 0.82 against 35.3 tok/s), so any floor catches it. An activation-only fallback costs roughly 1.2-2x; the review line and the recorded graph-splits line catch that case (INFERRED).
Today the floor uses only the 512-token decode, and the router's V10a figure comes from a 16-token reply, which is noise. A floor stated at 8k needs a small change to loadtest.py and to V10a.
Prefill floors: prefill is compute-bound, so it is the first place a lost GPU path shows. For GLM, below 40 tok/s at 8k a 24k-token document needs more than 13 min before the first word (INFERRED).

items.recommendation: Record 2,000 Mbps as the line figure. Neither the 10 GbE port nor Wi-Fi 7 is what limits the pull. Phase 3 fetches one file at a time over one curl stream, so it gets one stream's rate from Hugging Face's CDN. Set DOWNLOAD_MBPS=400 as a placeholder: about 2.5 h for the 448 GB Day 1 pull, 4.7 h for the 842 GB phased engines and 10.5 h for the 1.9 TB arsenal, against about 10, 19 and 42 h before. Before Phase 3, replace it with a 60-second single-stream download timed on the Principal's own line, because every sample so far comes from a US datacenter and the node is in Australia. Connect by cable from the 10 GbE port not marked DASH to a router port of 2.5 GbE or faster, and decide this before Phase 1. No script change is needed for Day 1. Parallel shard downloads are worth adding before the 842 GB phased pull.
reasons: The limit is the pull path, not the line. Phase 3 downloads each file over one curl connection, one file and one engine at a time, and hashes each file before starting the next. Single-stream samples from Hugging Face's CDN ran at 25-117 MB/s (researcher; median about 63 MB/s) and 92-96 MB/s (verifier, same file path). Four and eight parallel streams scaled almost linearly. One stream therefore gives roughly a quarter to a half of a 2 Gbps line.

Those samples were taken from a US cloud datacenter served by a Chicago CloudFront edge. The node is in Australia (doc L62). Hugging Face lists only US and EU CDN hosts, and the redirect targets xet-bridge-us, so an Australian edge that misses its cache fetches across the Pacific. The single-stream rate on the Principal's line is therefore UNVERIFIED and may be lower. A one-minute measurement settles it before the 448 GB pull starts.

None of the other settings named in the brief holds the pull back. The squid proxy has no SSL bump, no cache and no delay pools, and it does not set tcp_recv_bufsize (default 0 = OS default), so kernel TCP autotuning stays on. Its relay buffer of at most 64 KiB is a small load on one core at 250 MB/s. HF_HUB_ENABLE_HF_TRANSFER=0 does nothing here: curl never reads it, and huggingface_hub 1.0 and later ignore it. hf_xet is not used. Writes through LUKS run far below dm-crypt's speed.

The serial checksum adds time. On 26.04, sha256sum is the Rust uutils version, measured at about 136 MB/s (GNU at about 315 MB/s) on an unnamed CPU. With SHA-NI on Zen 5 it is probably 1 GB/s or more (UNVERIFIED). That adds 4 to 55 minutes to the 448 GB pull. The 400 Mbps placeholder comes from a single stream of about 63 MB/s plus a serial hash (344-487 Mbps effective), rounded down.

Wi-Fi 7 cannot carry the full 2 Gbps on this node. The RZ717 (MT7925) is limited to 160 MHz and 2.9 Gbps on paper. The measured best for a 2x2 160 MHz client is 1.62 Gbps with 6 parallel streams near the router, and 1.7-2.1 Gbps is only the blog author's estimate. A single stream measured 400 Mbps before that fix, and the pull is single-stream. A cable is limited only by the router port: a 1 GbE port gives about 941 Mbps, a 2.5 GbE or faster port passes the whole 2 Gbps.

The cable works on the 26.04 kernel. Linux 7.0's r8169 carries the RTL8127A family and handles its DASH variant explicitly (PCI revision 0x04 -> RTL_DASH_25_BP), and linux-firmware ships rtl_nic/rtl8127a-1.fw. Prefer the port not marked DASH and keep DASH off in the firmware setup. DASH is an out-of-band management path the OS firewall does not see (INFERRED).

The interface has to be chosen before Phase 1. LAN_IFACE is whichever interface carries the default route. DNS from dnsmasq, the outbound LAN rule and the Docker egress rules are tied to that interface. SSH, Cockpit and xrdp bind to its address, and the router's DHCP reservation and UDP 51820 forward follow one MAC address. A cable added after Phase 1 would therefore break name resolution, or do nothing. Reserve the same IP for the cable's MAC and take Wi-Fi off that subnet. The doc records 'Wi-Fi only by Principal's choice', so this is the Principal's decision.

Times for the 448 GB, 842 GB and 1.9 TB sets: 30 min, 56 min and 2 h 07 at 2,000 Mbps; 1 h 03, 1 h 59 and 4 h 29 at the 1 GbE cap; 2 h 29, 4 h 41 and 10 h 33 at the 400 Mbps placeholder (hash included); 5.0, 9.4 and 21.1 h if the Australian path delivers only 200 Mbps.

reasons: The stated D-16 default no longer fits. At the baseline's ~156 GiB budget (155.9-156.9) with the 2.0 GiB compute allowance, Q5_K_S leaves 3.06-4.06 GiB for the cache: 17,066-22,644 tokens at f16 (17,624 at 156.0). The 23K figure assumed the research's ~164 GiB budget. At 156 GiB the Arbiter would refuse 150.84 + 4.22 + 2.0 = 157.06 GiB.

Approved decision D-29 (a) already says 'f16 where the cache is cheap, q8_0 elsewhere'. At 192,512 B/token, about ten times GLM's 19,712, these seats fall under 'elsewhere'. So q8_0 applies the approved policy; it does not undo an approved decision. The baseline's '23K at f16' default was the inconsistency.
For the same bytes, q8_0 holds 1.88 times as many tokens (16 / 8.5): 3.12 GiB holds 32,768 tokens at q8_0 and 17,408 at f16.

Its quality cost is small next to dropping to 4-bit weights. llama.cpp discussion #23470 measured q8_0/q8_0 against f16 at a mean KLD of 0.0018 and 98.0% same top token (Qwen2.5-7B at 512 context), at most 4 of 500 ARC answers changed, and 0 flips in 1,600 deep-context comparisons up to 41K tokens. At 65K on Qwen3.8-27B the 99th-percentile KLD was 0.0064. For Qwen3-30B-A3B against BF16, Q4_K_M weights measured a KLD of 0.0101 and Q8_0 weights 0.0023. Q5_K_S + q8_0 should therefore stay below Q4_K_M + f16 (INFERRED). For Qwen3-235B, ik_llama's IQ5_K costs +0.63-0.75% perplexity against +1.21-1.37% for IQ4_K; these are proxies for the mainline rungs.

At the pin, a q8_0 cache on qwen3moe (head size 128) gets the Hadamard rotation automatically: n_rot_k = 128, n_rot_v = 64. The rotation matters: without it, a q8_0 cache cost gpt-oss-20b 6.2 AIME25 points (31.7% against 37.9% at f16); with it the score was 37.1%. Vulkan flash attention at the pin accepts Q8_0 K and V.

VERIFIER (new): at the pin, q8_0 is also the faster cache for long prompts on this hardware. A comment on llama.cpp PR #27703, from a Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 with 192 GB and kernel 7.0.0-38 (the node's configuration), measured prefill at 32K depth of 14.80 t/s with an f16 KV cache against 132.8 t/s with q8_0 (MiniMax M2.7). Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, which has the same 4 KV heads x 128 per layer as these seats, rose from 203 to 318 t/s at 32K once the post-pin fix was applied. The pin does not include that fix.

The 32K target is about what these seats will be asked to do. Today the cross-check prompt is only about 6-8K tokens: the draft, cut at 24,000 characters, plus the drafter's reasoning, with no sources and max_tokens 400. The 32K target covers two things: passing the cited sources once that is wired, and Baichuan's thinking (its card uses thinking on, max_new_tokens 32,768). Intern-S1 thinks by default and reads papers of roughly 8-15K tokens (INFERRED). About 17.6K tokens at f16 holds neither job together with its reasoning.

The target is 32,768 rather than 40,960 because 40,960 at Q5_K_S + q8_0 projects to 156.74 GiB under the 2 GiB planning allowance, above the expected budget. The real compute buffer at -ub 512 is probably 0.5-1.5 GiB (INFERRED), so 40,960 is likely reachable once it is measured.

reasons: On independent boards both existing seats beat Coder-Next by a wide margin. Artificial Analysis (AA): Terminal-Bench 2.1 84.27 (GLM) and 78.65 (V4-Flash-0731) against 38.20; Terminal-Bench 4.0 32.83 and 12.12 against 0.00; SciCode 51.62 and 50.35 against 36.23; Intelligence Index 41.81 and 34.33 against 9.24. GLM's 4-bit file (UD-IQ4_XS, KLD 0.117) is lossy, but no plausible loss brings it down to Coder-Next. To fall to Coder-Next's Terminal-Bench 2.1 score, GLM would have to lose 54.7% (46.07 / 84.27). VERIFIER: the 8.7% Flash-Next prune-and-quantise case is not the worst loss in the sources; the sources' own mapping puts about 6-9 points on Aider-style coding at KLD of 0.2 or more. GLM sits below that band, and even 9 points off leaves 92 - 9 = 83 on SWE-bench Verified against 71.1.

VERIFIER: GLM against V4-Flash-0731 is not settled by public scores. At the researcher's worst case (x 0.913), GLM falls to 84.0 on SWE-bench Verified against V4-Flash's 88.8 at near-lossless UD-Q8_K_XL, and to 76.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 against 78.65. V4-Flash also leads Vals LiveCodeBench, 87.26 against 80.51. GLM keeps Terminal-Bench 4.0 (32.83 against 12.12 on AA; 37.37 against 18.69 on Vals), decodes faster (12-17.4 against about 7 tok/s) and is the default resident seat (D-23), so it codes with no swap. This is why the T-03 coding set compares the two seats rather than only checking GLM's file for damage.

Coder-Next (released 2026-02-03) is a generation behind. Qwen's organisation has released no newer coder (newest Qwen repo 2026-10-09, an image model). Models released since 2026-10-15 change nothing: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B (AA 21.4, Terminal-Bench 4.0 0), Beam 1.0 501B (30.3; does not fit at 4-bit) and Muse Spark Open 816B (does not fit) all trail GLM.

Option (b), BF16, buys nothing. Measured on Coder-Next itself, perplexity is 8.2239 at Q8_0 and 8.2278 at BF16 (+/-0.064). BF16 decodes at about 9 tok/s against 37-44. With f16 KV under D-29 (a), a 256K window does not fit beside BF16 (156.58 GiB).
A dedicated seat adds a swap to every coding excursion: about 100-165 s to load Coder-Next and reload GLM, plus re-prefill.
A specialist earns a seat only where it beats the generalist (Ling-Fin on Finance Agent). Coder-Next does so on no independent board.

A 30-task set cannot resolve differences smaller than about +/-18-25 points at 95% confidence, so it cannot rescue Coder-Next, whose gaps are 15-46 points. Between GLM and V4-Flash it detects only a large regression, such as a damaged 4-bit file; smaller differences stay inside the noise.

reasons: Rad-DINO only turns chest X-rays into embeddings and writes no findings. MedGemma 1.5 4B drafts reads across chest X-ray, CT, MRI, whole-slide pathology, dermatology and fundus, including comparison with prior X-rays.

4B against 27B on imaging, both from Google's card: the 4B leads on 10 rows, among them CT 61.1/57.8, MRI 64.7/57.4, WSI 49.4/4.1, longitudinal CXR 65.7/50.1, anatomy IoU 38.0/16.0 and VQA-RAD closed 70.2/67.1. It trails by 1.7 points or less on MIMIC-CXR 89.5/90.0, CheXpert 48.2/49.9 and PathMCQA 70.0/71.6. The 27B leads clearly on SLAKE (F1 59.7/70.3, closed accuracy 82.8/85.9; the card blames the Q&A format) and on MedXpertQA (20.9/26.8). Report generation is level (RadGraph F1 27.2/27.0).

The 4B is faster: load in about 1.4-3.6 s, decode at about 21 tok/s, against 4.7-12.3 s and about 6 tok/s for the 27B.
BF16 follows the rule of the least-quantised rung that fits. Q8_0 is the fallback.
